172.content: 1 tn Heb &quot;of Nineveh.&quot; 2 tn Or &quot;Nahum of Elkosh&quot; (NAB, NRSV).

3 tn Heb &quot;jealous.&quot; The Hebrew term קַנּוֹא (qanno&apos;, &quot;jealous, zealous&quot;) refers to God&apos;s zealous protection of his people and his furious judgment against his enemies. The root קָנָא (qana&apos;) can denote jealous envy (Gen 26:14; 30:1; 37:11; Pss 37:1; 73:3; 106:16; Prov 3:31; 23:17; 24:1, 19; Ezek 31:9), jealous rivalry (Eccl 4:4; 9:6; Isa 11:13), marital jealousy (Num 5:14, 15, 18, 25, 30; Prov 6:34; 27:4), zealous loyalty (Num 11:29; 25:11, 13; 2 Sam 21:2; 1 Kgs 19:10, 14; 2 Kgs 10:16; Ps 69:10; Song 8:6; Isa 9:6; 37:32; 42:13; 59:17; 63:15; Zech 1:14; 8:2), jealous anger (Deut 32:16, 21; Ps 78:58), and zealous fury (Exod 34:14; Deut 5:9; 29:19; 1 Kgs 14:22; Job 5:2; Pss 79:5; 119:139; Prov 14:30; Isa 26:11; Ezek 5:13; 8:3; 16:38, 42; 23:25; 35:11; 36:5, 6; 38:19; Zeph 1:18). See BDB 888 s.v. קָנָא; E. Reuter, TDOT 13:47-58. 4 tn The syntax of this line has been understood in two ways: (1) as a single clause with the Lord as the subject: &quot;A jealous and avenging God is the Lord&quot; (NRSV; NASB) or &quot;The Lord is a jealous and avenging God&quot; (NIV); and (2) as two parallel clauses: &quot;God is jealous, and the Lord avenges&quot; (KJV). The LXX reflects the latter. Masoretic accentuation and Hebrew syntax support the former. Accentuation links קַנּוֹא וְנֹקֵם (qano&apos; vÿnoqem, &quot;jealous and avenging&quot;) together rather than dividing them into separate clauses. Normal word order suggests that קַנּוֹא וְנֹקֵם (&quot;jealous and avenging&quot;) are attributive adjectives modifying אֵל (&apos;el, &quot;God&quot;). In verbless clauses such as this, the predicate normally precedes the subject; thus, &quot;a jealous and avenging God&quot; (אֵל קַנּוֹא וְנֹקֵם, &apos;el qanno&apos; vÿnoqem) is the predicate and &quot;the Lord&quot; (יְהוָה, yÿhvah) is the subject. 5 tn Or &quot;exceedingly wrathful&quot;; Heb &quot;a lord of wrath.&quot; The idiom &quot;lord of wrath&quot; (וּבַעַל חֵמָה, uva&apos;al khemah) means &quot;wrathful&quot; or &quot;full of wrath&quot; (Prov 22:24; 29:22). The noun &quot;lord&quot; (בַעַל) is used in construct as an idiom to describe a person&apos;s outstanding characteristic or attribute (e.g., Gen 37:19; 1 Sam 28:7; 2 Kgs 1:8; Prov 1:17; 18:9; 22:24; 23:2; 24:8; Eccl 7:12; 8:8; 10:11, 20; Isa 41:15; 50:8; Dan 8:6, 20); see IBHS 149-51 §9.5.3. 6 tn The term נָקַם (naqam, &quot;avenge, vengeance&quot;) is used three times in 1:2 for emphasis. The Lord will exact just retribution against his enemies (the Assyrians) to avenge their wickedness against his people (Judah). 7 tn The verb &quot;rage&quot; (נָטַר, natar) is used elsewhere of keeping a vineyard (Song 1:6; 8:11-12) and guarding a secret (Dan 7:28). When used of anger, it does not so much mean &quot;to control anger&quot; or &quot;to be slow to anger&quot; (HALOT 695 s.v.) but &quot;to stay angry&quot; (TWOT 2:576). It describes a person bearing a grudge, seeking revenge, and refusing to forgive (Lev 19:18). It is often used as a synonym of שָׁמַר (shamar, &quot;to maintain wrath, stay angry&quot;) in collocation with לְעוֹלָם (lÿ&apos;olam, &quot;forever, always&quot;) and לָעַד (la&apos;ad, &quot;continually&quot;) to picture God harboring rage against his enemies forever (Jer 3:5, 12; Amos 1:11; Ps 103:9). The long-term rage depicted by נָטַר (&quot;maintain rage&quot;) serves as an appropriate bridge to the following statement in Nahum that the Lord is slow to anger but furious in judgment. God seeks vengeance against his enemies; he continually rages and maintains his anger; he is slow to anger, but will eventually burst out with the full fury of his wrath.

8 tn Heb &quot;long of anger,&quot; i.e., &quot;slow to anger&quot; (Exod 34:6; Num 14:18; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Pss 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Prov 14:29; 15:18; 16:32; Neh 9:17) or restraining anger (Jer 15:15; Prov 25:15). Cf. NCV &quot;The Lord does not become angry quickly.&quot; 9 tc The BHS editors suggest emending MT &quot;power&quot; (כֹּחַ, koakh) to &quot;mercy&quot; (חֶסֶד, khesed) as in Exod 34:6; Num 14:18; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Ps 103:8; Neh 9:17. However, this is unnecessary, it has no textual support, and it misses the rhetorical point intended by Nahum&apos;s modification of the traditional expression. sn This is an allusion to the well-known statement, &quot;The Lord is slow to anger but great in mercy&quot; (Exod 34:6; Num 14:18; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Ps 103:8; Neh 9:17). Nahum subtly modifies this by substituting &quot;great in mercy&quot; with &quot;great in power.&quot; God&apos;s patience at the time of Jonah (Jonah 4:2) one century earlier (ca. 750 b.c.), had run out. Nineveh had exhausted the &quot;great mercy&quot; of God and now would experience the &quot;great power&quot; of God. 10 tn Or &quot;he will certainly not acquit [the wicked]&quot;; KJV &quot;and will not at all acquit the wicked.&quot; The root נָקַה (naqah, &quot;to acquit&quot;) is repeated for emphasis. The phrase &quot;he will certainly not allow the wicked to go unpunished&quot; (וְנַקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה, vÿnaqqeh lo&apos; yÿnaqqeh) is an emphatic construction (see GKC 215 §75.hh; IBHS 584-88 §35.3.1). 11 tn The words &quot;the wicked&quot; are not in the Hebrew text but are supplied in the translation; they are implied when this idiom is used (Exod 34:7; Num 14:18). In legal contexts the nuance &quot;the guilty&quot; is most appropriate; in nonlegal contexts the nuance &quot;the wicked&quot; is used. 12 tn Heb &quot;His way is in the whirlwind&quot; (so NIV). The noun דַּרְכּוֹ (darko, &quot;his way&quot;) is nuanced here in a verbal sense. The noun דֶּרֶךְ (derekh) often denotes a &quot;journey&quot; (Gen 28:20; 30:36; 45:23; Num 9:10; Josh 9:13; 1 Sam 21:6; 1 Kgs 18:27). The verb דָּרַךְ (darakh) often means &quot;to tread a path&quot; (Job 22:15) and &quot;to march out&quot; (Judg 5:21). The Lord is portrayed as the Divine Warrior marching out to battle (Exod 15:1-12; Deut 33:2; Judg 5:4-5; Pss 18:7-15; 68:4-10, 32-35; 77:16-19; Mic 1:3-4; Hab 3:3-15). 13 tn Heb &quot;clouds are dust.&quot; 14 tn Heb &quot;of his feet.&quot;

15 tn The term גָּעַר (ga&apos;ar) often denotes &quot;reprimand&quot; and &quot;rebuke&quot; (cf. KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV). When it is used in the context of a military attack, it denotes an angry battle cry shouted by a mighty warrior to strike fear into his enemies to drive them away (e.g., 2 Sam 23:16; Isa 30:17; Pss 18:15; 76:6; 80:17; 104:7). For example, the parallel Ugaritic term is used when Baal utters a battle cry against Yamm before they fight to the death. For further study see, A. A. MacIntosh, &quot;A Consideration of Hebrew g`r,&quot; VT 14 (1969): 474; P. J. van Zijl, &quot;A Consideration of the root ga&apos;ar (&quot;rebuke&quot;),&quot; OTWSA 12 (1969): 56-63; A. Caquot, TDOT 3:49-53. 16 sn The &quot;sea&quot; is personified as an antagonistic enemy, representing the wicked forces of chaos (Pss 66:6; 72:8; 80:12; 89:26; 93:3-4; Isa 50:2; Mic 7:12; Hab 3:8; Zech 9:10). 17 tn This somewhat unusual use of the preterite (וַיַּבְּשֵׁהוּ, vayyabbÿshehu) follows a participle which depicts characteristic (present-time) action or imminent future action; the preterite depicts the subsequent present or future-time action (see IBHS 561-62 §33.3.5). 18 sn The Assyrians waged war every spring after the Tigris and Euphrates rivers dried up, allowing them to cross. As the Mighty Warrior par excellence, the Lord is able to part the rivers to attack Assyria. 19 tn The term אֻמְלַל (&apos;umlal, &quot;withers&quot;) occurs twice in this verse in MT. The repetition of אֻמְלַל is also supported by the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QpNah). The BHS editors suggest emending the first occurrence of אֻמְלַל (&quot;withers&quot;) to דָּלְלוּ (dollu, &quot;languishes&quot;) to recover the letter ד (dalet) in the partial acrostic. Several versions do, in fact, employ two different verbs in the line (LXX, Syr, Targum, and Vg). However, the first verb at the beginning of the line in all of the versions reflects a reading of אֻמְלַל. Although several elements of an acrostic are present in Nahum 1, the acrostic is incomplete (only א [alef] to כ [kaf] in vv. 2-8) and broken (several elements are missing within vv. 2-8). There is no textual evidence for a complete, unbroken acrostic throughout the book of Nahum in any ancient Hebrew mss or other textual versions; it is most prudent simply to leave the MT as it stands.

20 tn Or &quot;because of him.&quot; The Hebrew preposition מִמֶּנּוּ (mimmenu) is taken in a causal sense (&quot;because of him&quot;) by NASB, NJPS; however, it is taken in a locative sense (&quot;before him&quot;) by KJV, NKJV, NRSV, NIV. On the other hand, the LXX rendered it in a separative sense: ἀπ&apos; αὐτοῦ (ap autou, &quot;from him&quot;). The parallelism between 1:5a and 1:5b seems to favor the locative nuance: &quot;The mountains quake before him (מִמֶּנּוּ), the earth is laid waste before him (מִפָּנָיו, mifanayv).&quot; 21 tn Traditionally, &quot;the hills melt.&quot; English versions typically render הִתְמֹגָגוּ (hitmogagu) as &quot;melt&quot; (KJV, NRSV, NIV, NJPS) or &quot;dissolve&quot; (NASB). The LXX renders it ἐσαλεύθησαν (esaleuqhsan, &quot;are shaken&quot;). The Hebrew root has a range of meanings: (1) &quot;to melt,&quot; of courage (Ps 107:26) or troops retreating (&quot;melting away&quot; in fear) in battle (1 Sam 14:16); (2) &quot;to dissolve,&quot; of mountains dissolving due to erosion (Amos 9:13); (3) &quot;to quake, shake apart,&quot; of mountains quaking, swaying backwards and forwards, coming apart, and collapsing in an earthquake (Amos 9:5; Pss 46:6 [7]; 75:3 [4]). The latter fits the imagery of v. 5 (violent earthquakes): the earth trembles in fear at the approach of the Divine Warrior (e.g., Hab 3:6). 22 tn Or &quot;is upheaved&quot;; or &quot;heaves.&quot; There is debate whether the originally unpointed Hebrew verb וַתִּשָּׂא (vattissa&apos;) should be vocalized as וְתִּשָּׂא (vÿttissa&apos;; NASB &quot;is upheaved&quot;; NRSV, NJPS &quot;heaves&quot;) from the root נָשָׂא (nasa&apos;, &quot;to lift up&quot;) or as וַתִּשָּׁא (vattisha&apos;, &quot;is devastated, laid waste&quot;) from the root שֹׁאָה (sho&apos;ah, &quot;to devastate, lay waste&quot;). The vocalization וְתִּשָּׂא is attested in the Masoretic tradition and the Greek versions: Origen (&quot;was raised up&quot;), Symmachus (&quot;was moved&quot;), and Aquila (&quot;shivered&quot;). However, וְתִּשָּׂא demands an intransitive (&quot;heaves&quot;) or passive (&quot;is upheaved&quot;) sense which is not attested for the Qal stem. The vocalization וַתִּשָּׁא (&quot;is devastated, laid waste&quot;) is supported by the Syriac and Vulgate. The revocalization of the MT וְתִּשָּׂא (&quot;is lifted up&quot;) to וַתִּשָּׁא (&quot;is devastated&quot;) is suggested by the BHS editors and several Hebrew lexicons (HALOT 726 s.v. נשׁא; BDB 670-71 s.v. נָשָׂא). The revocalization involves only the difference between the form שׂ (sin) and שׁ (shin) and is followed in the present translation. 23 sn The phrase &quot;the world and all its inhabitants&quot; is used to stress the universal dimensions of God&apos;s revelation of his glory and his acts of judgment (e.g., Pss 33:8; 98:7; Isa 18:3; 26:9, 18; Lam 4:12). 24 tn The words &quot;are laid waste&quot; are not in the Hebrew text, but are an implied repetition from the previous line.

25 tn Heb &quot;stand before&quot; (so KJV, NASB, NRSV, NLT). The Hebrew verb עָמַד (&apos;amad, &quot;stand&quot;) here denotes &quot;to resist, withstand.&quot; It is used elsewhere of warriors taking a stand in battle to hold their ground against enemies (Judg 2:14; Josh 10:8; 21:44; 23:9; 2 Kgs 10:4; Dan 11:16; Amos 2:15). It is also used of people trying to protect their lives from enemy attack (Esth 8:11; 9:16). Like a mighty warrior, the Lord will attack his enemies, but none will be able to make a stand against him; none will be able to hold their ground against him; and none will be able to protect themselves from his onslaught (Pss 76:7[8]; 147:17; Mal 3:2). 26 tn Heb &quot;Who can stand before his indignation?&quot; The rhetorical question expects a negative answer; it is translated here as an emphatic denial. The Hebrew noun זַעַם (za&apos;am, &quot;indignation, curse&quot;) connotes the angry wrath or indignant curse of God (Isa 10:5, 25; 13:5; 26:20; 30:27; Jer 10:10; 15:17; 50:25; Ezek 21:36; 22:24, 31; Hab 3:12; Zeph 3:8; Pss 38:4; 69:25; 78:49; 102:11; Lam 2:6; Dan 8:19; 11:36). It depicts anger expressed in the form of punishment (HALOT 276 s.v.; TWOT 1:247). 27 tn Heb &quot;Who can rise up against...?&quot; The verb יָקוּם (yaqum, &quot;arise&quot;) is here a figurative expression connoting resistance. Although the adversative sense of בְּ (bet) with יָקוּם (yaqum, &quot;against him&quot;) is attested, denoting hostile action taken against one&apos;s enemy (Mic 7:6; Ps 27:12), the locative sense (&quot;before him&quot;) is preferred due to the parallelism with לִפְנֵי (lifney, &quot;before him&quot;). 28 tn Heb &quot;Who can rise up against the heat of his anger?&quot; The rhetorical question expects a negative answer which is translated as an emphatic denial to clarify the point. 29 tn Or &quot;burst into flames.&quot; The Niphal perfect נִתְּצוּ (nittÿtsu) from נָתַץ (natats, &quot;to break up, throw down&quot;) may denote &quot;are broken up&quot; or &quot;are thrown down.&quot; The BHS editors suggest emending the MT&apos;s נִתְּצוּ (nittÿtsu) to נִצְּתּוּ (nitsÿtu, Niphal perfect from יָצַת [yatsat, &quot;to burn, to kindle, to burst into flames&quot;]): &quot;boulders burst into flames.&quot; This merely involves the simple transposition of the second and third consonants. This emendation is supported by a few Hebrew mss (cited in BHS apparatus). It is supported contextually by fire and heat motifs in 1:5-6. The same metathesis of נִתְּצוּ and נִצְּתּוּ occurs in Jer 4:26. 30 tn Heb &quot;before him&quot; (so NAB, NIV, TEV).

31 tn The Masoretic disjunctive accent marker (zaqeph parvum) divides the lines here. Most English versions reflect this line division (KJV, RSV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NKJV). Some extend the line: &quot;Yahweh is better than a fortress&quot; (NJB); &quot;The Lord is good to those who hope in him&quot; (NJPS); and &quot;The Lord is good to those who trust him&quot; (NEB). This issue is complicated by the textual problems in this verse. 32 tn The preposition לְ (lamed) probably functions in an emphatic asseverative sense, suggested by D. L. Christensen, &quot;The Acrostic of Nahum Reconsidered,&quot; ZAW 87 (1975): 22. This explains the preceding statement: the Lord is good to his people (1:7a) because - like a fortress - he protects them in time of distress (1:7b). 33 tc Some ancient versions read, &quot;The Lord is good to those who trust him.&quot; The MT reads לְמָעוֹז (lÿma&apos;oz, &quot;a fortress&quot;): the noun מָעוֹז (ma&apos;oz, &quot;fortress&quot;) with the preposition לְ (lÿ, see below). However, the LXX reflects the reading לְמֵעִיז (lÿme&apos;iz, &quot;to those who trust [him]&quot;): the Hiphil participle from עוּז (&apos;uz, &quot;seek refuge&quot;) with the preposition לְ. The variants involve only different vocalizations and the common confusion of vav (ו) with yod. Most English versions follow the traditional Hebrew reading (KJV, RSV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NKJV); however, several others follow the alternate Greek reading (NEB, NJPS). The BHS editors and several other scholars favor the LXX tradition; however, the Masoretic tradition has been defended by others. The Masoretic tradition is supported by the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QpNah). The problem with the LXX reading is the absence of the direct object in the Hebrew text; the LXX is forced to supply the direct object αὐτόν (auton, &quot;him&quot;; for a similar addition of the direct object αὐτόν by the LXX, see Amos 9:12). The main objection to the MT reading לְמָעוֹז (&quot;a fortress&quot;) is that לְ is hard to explain. However, לְ may be taken in a comparative sense (Cathcart: &quot;Yahweh is better than a fortress in time of distress&quot;) or an asseverative sense (Christensen: &quot;Yahweh is good; indeed, a fortress in time of distress&quot;). See K. J. Cathcart, Nahum in the Light of Northwest Semitic (BibOr), 55; idem, &quot;More Philological Studies in Nahum,&quot; JNSL 7 (1979): 4; D. L. Christensen, &quot;The Acrostic of Nahum Reconsidered,&quot; ZAW 87 (1975): 22. Elsewhere, the Lord is commonly portrayed as a &quot;fortress&quot; (מָעוֹז) protecting his people (Pss 27:1; 28:8; 31:3, 5; 37:39; 43:2; 52:9; Isa 17:10; 25:4; 27:5; Joel 4:16; Jer 16:19; Neh 8:10; Prov 10:29). 34 sn The phrase &quot;time of distress&quot; (בְּיוֹם צָרָה) refers to situations in which God&apos;s people are oppressed by enemy armies (Isa 33:2; Jer 14:8; 15:11; 16:19; Obad 12; Pss 20:2; 37:39). Nahum may be alluding to recent Assyrian invasions of Judah, such as Sennacherib&apos;s devastating invasion in 701 b.c., in which the Lord protected the remnant within the fortress walls of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18-19; 2 Chr 32; Isa 36-37). 35 tn Heb &quot;he knows&quot; or &quot;he recognizes.&quot; The basic meaning of the verb יָדַע (yada&apos;) is &quot;to know,&quot; but it may denote &quot;to take care of someone&quot; or &quot;to protect&quot; (HALOT 391 s.v.; see Gen 39:6; Job 9:21; Ps 31:8). Most English versions render it as &quot;know&quot; here (KJV, RSV, NASB, NKJV) but at least two recognize the nuance &quot;protect&quot; (NRSV, NIV [which reads &quot;cares for&quot;]). It often refers to God protecting and caring for his people (2 Sam 7:20; Ps 144:3). When the subject is a king (suzerain) and the object is a servant (vassal), it often has covenantal overtones. In several ancient Near Eastern languages this term depicts the king (suzerain) recognizing his treaty obligation to protect and rescue his servant (vassal) from its enemies. For example, a letter from Abdi-Ashirta governor of Ammuru to the Egyptian king Amenophis III ends with a plea for protection from the raids of the Mittani: &quot;May the king my lord know [= protect] me&quot; (yi-da-an-ni; EA 60:30-32). Similarly, in the treaty between Muwattallis and Alaksandus, the Hittite suzerain assures his vassal that in case he was attacked, &quot;As he is an enemy of you, even so he is an enemy to the Sun; I the Sun, will know [= &quot;protect&quot;] only you, Alaksandus&quot; (see H. B. Huffmon, &quot;The Treaty Background of Hebrew YADA`,&quot; BASOR 181 (1966): 31-37; idem, &quot;A Further Note on the Treaty Background of Hebrew YADA`,&quot; BASOR 184 (1966): 36-38. 36 tn Or &quot;those who trust in him&quot; (NIV); NAB &quot;those who have recourse to him.&quot;

37 tn Some scholars connect &quot;in an overwhelming flood&quot; (וּבְשֶׁטֶף עֹבֵר, uvÿshetef &apos;over) with the preceding line: &quot;he protects those who trust him in an overwhelming flood.&quot; However, others connect it with the following line: &quot;But with an overwhelming flood he will make a complete end of its [Nineveh&apos;s] site.&quot; D. T. Tsumura (&quot;Janus Parallelism in Nah 1:8,&quot; JBL 102 [1983]: 109-11) suggests that it does double duty and should be read with both lines: &quot;he knows those who trust him in an overwhelming flood, / but with an overwhelming flood he will make a complete end of its [Nineveh&apos;s] site.&quot; Connecting it with the preceding line creates a tight parallelism and a balanced 5+5 metrical count. Connecting it with the following line harmonizes with Nah 2:9 [8], which describes the walls of Nineveh being destroyed by flood waters, and with historical evidence (Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica, 2.27.1-3; Xenophon, Anabasis, 3.4.12) and modern archaeological evidence (A. T. Olmstead, History of Assyria, 637). This might be an example of intentional ambiguity: God will protect his people from the very calamity that he will use to destroy his enemies. 38 tc Heb &quot;her place.&quot; Alternately, some ancient versions read &quot;his adversaries.&quot; The MT reads מְקוֹמָהּ (mÿqomah, &quot;her place&quot;). This is supported by the Dead Sea Scrolls (מקומה, &quot;her place,&quot; found in 4QpNah) and Symmachus (τῆς τόποῦ αὐτοῦ, th&quot; topou autou, &quot;her place&quot;). The reading of the LXX (τούς ἐπεγειρουμένους, tou&quot; epegeiroumenou&quot;, &quot;those who rise up [against Him]&quot;) and Aquila (ἀντισταμενω¡ν, antistamenw&gt;n, &quot;adversaries&quot;) reflect מְקּוֹמיהוּ or מְקִימיהוּ or מְקִּמָיו (&quot;his adversaries&quot;), also reflected in the Vulgate and Targum. Some scholars suggest emending the MT in the light of the LXX to create a tight parallelism between &quot;his adversaries&quot; (מקומיו) and &quot;his enemies&quot; (וְאֹיְבָיו, vÿ&apos;oyÿvayv) which is a parallel word pair elsewhere (Deut 28:7; 2 Sam 22:40-41, 49; Mic 7:6; Ps 59:2). Likewise, Tsumura suggests emending the MT because the text, as it stands, does not have a clear parallel word for &quot;his enemies&quot; (וְאֹיְבָיו) - emending the MT&apos;s מְקוֹמָהּ (&quot;her place&quot;) to מקומיו (&quot;his adversaries&quot;) would result in a parallel word (D. T. Tsumura, &quot;Janus Parallelism in Nah 1:8,&quot; JBL 102 [1983]: 109-11). The BHS editors propose emending the MT in favor of the Greek tradition. The English versions reflect both textual traditions - several follow the MT with &quot;her place&quot; and &quot;its site&quot; (KJV, NASB, NIV, NKJV, NJPS), while others adopt the LXX reading and emend the Hebrew, resulting in &quot;his adversaries&quot; (NRSV) or &quot;those who defy him&quot; (NJB). The MT makes sense as it stands, but the proposed emendation is attractive and involves only the common confusion between ה and יו. 39 tc The BHS editors propose emending the Masoretic reading יְרַדֶּף (yÿraddef, Piel imperfect of רָדַּף [raddaf], &quot;to chase&quot;) to יֶהְדֹּף (yekhdof, Qal imperfect of הָדַף [hadaf], &quot;to thrust away, drive away&quot;). Although הָדַף is used with חֹשֶׁךְ (khoshekh, &quot;darkness&quot;) in Job 18:18 (&quot;he is driven from light into darkness&quot;), the MT makes good sense as it stands, and is supported by the versions. The conjectural emendation has no support and is unnecessary.

40 tn Alternately, &quot;Why are you plotting?&quot; or &quot;What are you plotting?&quot; The term מַה (mah) ordinarily functions as the interrogative pronoun &quot;what?&quot; (HALOT 550-51 s.v.; BDB 552-53 s.v.). It is often used in reproachful, ridiculing questions and in accusations with an insinuation of blame, reproach, or contempt; see Gen 4:10; 37:10; 44:15; Josh 22:16; Judg 8:1; 15:11; 20:12; 1 Sam 29:3; 2 Sam 9:8; 1 Kgs 9:13; 2 Kgs 9:22; 18:19). It is more disparaging than מִי (mi; HALOT 551 s.v. מַה). The LXX translates it with the interrogative pronoun τί (&quot;what?&quot;). R. L. Smith (Micah-Malachi [WBC], 76) takes it as the indefinite pronoun &quot;whatever&quot; (see also BDB 553 s.v. מָה 3; GKC 443-44 §137.c; Num 23:3; 1 Sam 19:3; 20:10; 2 Sam 18:22-23, 29; Job 13:13; Prov 25:8). W. A. Maier (Nahum, 186) takes it as the interrogative adverb &quot;why?&quot; (see also BDB 553 s.v. מָה 2.b; Gen 3:13; 12:18; 26:10; Exod 14:15; 17:2; 2 Kgs 6:33; 7:3; Pss 42:6, 12; 43:5; 52:3; Job 7:21; 15:12; Song 8:4). All three are represented in English versions: &quot;What?&quot; (KJV, NKJV), &quot;Why?&quot; (NRSV, NJPS), and &quot;Whatever&quot; (NASB, NIV). 41 tn Less likely, &quot;[What are you] thinking about.&quot; When used with אֶל (&apos;el) the verb חָשַׁב (khashav) may be taken (1) in a hostile sense: &quot;What are you plotting against the Lord?&quot; or (2) in a nonhostile sense: &quot;What are you thinking about the Lord?&quot; The hostile sense is clearly intended when it is used in collocation with the direct object רָעָה (ra&apos;ah, &quot;evil&quot;; Zech 7:10; 8:17; Pss 35:4; 140:3; Prov 16:9) or when it is followed by the preposition עַל (&apos;al; Gen 50:20; 2 Sam 14:13; Jer 11:19; 18:11, 18; 29:11; 48:2; 49:30; Mic 2:3; Nah 1:11; Pss 36:5; Esth 8:3; 9:24, 25; Dan 11:25). It is also used in a hostile sense when followed by the preposition אֶל, as it is here (Jer 49:20; 50:45; Hos 7:15; Nah 1:9). The major lexicons classify this usage in a hostile sense (BDB 363 s.v. חָשַׁב; HALOT 360 s.v. חשׁב). The verb is repeated in Nah 1:11 where it is clearly used in a hostile sense. 42 tn Or &quot;The Lord will completely foil whatever you plot against him&quot;; or &quot;Whatever you may think about the Lord, he [always] brings everything to a conclusion.&quot; 43 tc The MT reads צָרָה (tsarah, &quot;distress&quot;). This is supported by the LXX. However, the BHS editors propose emending the MT&apos;s צָרָה (&quot;distress&quot;) to צָרָיו (tsarayv, &quot;his adversaries&quot;). Several English versions follow course (NRSV, NJPS); however, the majority of English versions follow the traditional MT reading (KJV, NASB, NIV, NKJV). The term &quot;distress&quot; (צָרָה, tsarah) is repeated from v. 7: God will not only protect his people in time of &quot;distress&quot; (צָרָה) from the Assyrians (v. 7), he will put an end to &quot;distress&quot; (צָרָה) by destroying the Assyrians (v. 9). 44 tn The originally unvocalized consonantal form תקום is vocalized in the MT as תָקוּם (taqum, &quot;will arise&quot;) from קוּם (qum, &quot;to arise&quot;). However, the LXX reflects a vocalization of תִקּוֹם (tiqom, &quot;will take vengeance&quot;) from נָקַם (naqam, &quot;to avenge&quot;). The Masoretic vocalization makes sense and should be retained. The LXX vocalization probably arose under the influence of the three-fold repetition of נקם in Nah 1:2.

45 tn The verb אֻכְּלוּ (&apos;ukkÿlu, &quot;they will be consumed&quot;) is an example of the old Qal passive perfect 3rd person common plural which was erroneously pointed by the Masoretes as Pual perfect 3rd person common plural. The Qal passive of אָכַל (&apos;akhal) occurs several times in the Hebrew Bible, pointed as Pual (e.g., Exod 3:2; Neh 2:3, 13; Isa 1:20; Nah 1:10). For further discussion on the old Qal passive see H. L. Ginsberg, &quot;Studies on the Biblical Hebrew Verb: Masoretically Misconstrued Internal Passives,&quot; AJSL 46 (1929): 53-56; R. J. Williams, &quot;The Passive Qal Theme in Hebrew,&quot; Essays on the Ancient Semitic World, 43-50; Joüon 1:166-67 §58.a; IBHS 373-76 §22.6 (see especially n. 36 on p. 375). 46 tn The particle עַד (&apos;ad) is taken as a comparative of degree (&quot;like&quot;) by many lexicographers (BDB 724 s.v. I.3; HALOT 787 s.v. 5), English versions (NASB, NRSV, NJPS), and scholars (W. A. Maier, Nahum, 192; R. L. Smith, Micah-Malachi [WBC], 76; R. D. Patterson, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah [WEC], 42). Although the comparative sense is rare (1 Sam 11:15; 2 Sam 23:19; 2 Kgs 24:20; 1 Chr 4:27), it is suggested by the similes in v. 10 (see R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 57, §312). The comparative sense is reflected in the Greek versions of Symmachus, Aquila, and Theodotion. Although Origen took עַד in its more common spatial sense (&quot;up to&quot;), his approach can be dismissed because he misunderstood the entire line: ὅτι ἕως θεμελίου αὐτοῦ ξερσωθήσεται (Joti Jew&quot; qemeliou autou xerswqhsetai, &quot;up to his foundation he shall be laid bare&quot;). The KJV takes עַד in its rare temporal sense (&quot;while&quot;; see BDB 725 s.v. II.2). T. Longman suggests a locative sense: &quot;by the entangled thorns they are like drunkards stinking of drink&quot; (&quot;Nahum,&quot; The Minor Prophets, 2:794, 796; see R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 56-57, §310). Because of its difficulty, several scholars have resorted to conjectural emendations of the MT: (1) K. J. Cathcart (Nahum in the Light of Northwest Semitic [BibOr], 61) suggests emending the MT&apos;s עַד to the temporal particle עוֹד (&apos;od, &quot;again&quot;); (2) The BHS editors suggest emending the MT&apos;s כִּי עַד (ki &apos;ad) to הוֹי עִיר (hoy &apos;ir, &quot;woe to the city!&quot;) which appears in Nah 3:1; (3) The BHS editors suggest the alternate conjectural emendation of יִבְעֲרוּ כְ (yiv&apos;aru kÿ, &quot;they will burn like ...&quot;); (4) H. Junker (Die zwolf kleinen Propheten, 175) suggests emending כִּי עַד (ki &apos;ad) to כְּיַעַד (kÿya&apos;ad, &quot;like a forest&quot;). Although the Masoretic reading is difficult, it is more plausible than any conjectural emendation. 47 tc The MT reads סִירִים סְבֻכִים (sirim sÿvukhim, &quot;entangled thorn-bushes&quot;), and is supported by the Dead Sea text from Murabba`at: סירים סבכים (see DJD 2:197). The noun סִירִים (&quot;thorn bushes&quot;) is from סִיר (sir, &quot;thorn, thorn bush,&quot; BDB 696 s.v. II סִיר; HALOT 752 s.v. *סִירָה), e.g., Isa 34:13; Hos 2:8; Eccl 7:6. The Qal passive participle סְבֻכִים (sÿvukhim) is from סָבַךְ (savakh, &quot;to interweave,&quot; BDB 687 s.v. סָבַךְ; HALOT 740 s.v. סבך), e.g., Job 8:17, which is related to Assyrian sabaku (&quot;to entwine,&quot; AHw 2:999.a) and Arabic sabaka (&quot;to entwine&quot;; Leslau, 51). The MT is supported by several LXX translators, e.g., Symmachus, Aquila, and Theodotion. It is also reflected in Vulgate&apos;s spinarum perplexi (&quot;thorn-bushes entangled&quot;). On the other hand, the Syriac Peshitta reflects סָרִים סוֹרְרִים (sarim sorÿrim, &quot;your princes are rebels&quot;) which points to orthographic confusion and a different vocalization. Similar textual confusion is apparent in Origen: θεμελίου αὐτοῦ ξερσωθήσεται (qemeliou autou xerswqhsetai, &quot;his foundation shall be laid bare&quot;) seems to reflect יְסֹדָם יְכָבֵּס (yÿsodam yÿkhabbes, &quot;their foundation shall be washed away&quot;) which was caused by orthographic confusion and transposition of consonants. The MT should be retained. sn This simile compares the imminent destruction of Nineveh to the burning of a mass of entangled thorn-bushes (Job 8:17). When thorn-bushes are entangled they burn quickly and completely ( Eccl 7:6; Isa 34:13). 48 tc The MT reading וּכְסָבְאָם סְבוּאִים (ukhÿsav&apos;am sÿvu&apos;im, &quot;and like the drink of drunkards&quot;) is supported by Symmachus (&quot;and as those drinking their drink with one another&quot;) who is known for his wooden literalness to the Hebrew text, and by Vulgate which reads et sicut vino suo inebriati. K. J. Cathcart revocalizes as וּכְסֹבְאִים סְבֻאִים (ukhÿsovÿ&apos;im sÿvu&apos;im, &quot;and like drunkards sodden with drink&quot;; Nahum in the Light of Northwest Semitic [BibOr], 61). Haldar equates Hebrew סָבָא (sava&apos;) with Ugaritic sp&apos; (&quot;eat&quot;) due to an interchange between ב (bet) and פ (pe), and produces &quot;and as they consume a consuming&quot; (A. Haldar, Studies in the Book of Nahum, 32). Barr argues that the mem (מ) on MT וּכְסָבְאָם (ukhÿsov&apos;am) is enclitic, and he translates the line as &quot;and as the drunken are getting drunk&quot; (J. Barr, Comparative Philology, 33). tn The MT&apos;s וּכְסָבְאָם is a noun with masculine plural suffix from סֹבֶא (sove&apos;, &quot;drink, liquor&quot;), meaning &quot;their drink, liquor&quot; (e.g., Hos 4:18). This is supported by Symmachus (&quot;their drink&quot;) and is reflected in the Syriac (&quot;in their drink&quot;). The Masoretic סְבוּאִים (sÿvu&apos;im) is the passive participle from סָבָא (sava&apos;, &quot;to drink,&quot; BDB 684-85 s.v. סָבָא). This produces &quot;and like their liquor/drink being drunken.&quot; This makes good sense with the following line in which אֻכְּלוּ (&apos;ukkÿlu, &quot;they will be consumed&quot;) appears. The verb אֻכְּלוּ is frequently used in comparisons of consuming liquor and being consumed like chaff. 49 tc The BHS editors propose emending the MT&apos;s מָלֵא (male&apos;, &quot;fully&quot;) to the negative interrogative הֲלֹא (halo&apos;, &quot;Has not...?&quot;) and connecting it with the next line: &quot;Has not one plotting evil marched out from you?&quot; However, this emendation is unnecessary because the MT makes sense as it stands, and there is no textual support for the emendation. The MT is supported by the Greek tradition, the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QpNah), and the other versions. tn Or &quot;They will be fully consumed like dried stubble.&quot; The term מָלֵא (&quot;fully&quot;) functions either as: (1) an adjective modifying כְּקַשׁ יָבֵשׁ (kÿqash yavesh, &quot;like fully dried stubble&quot;) or (2) an adverb modifying אֻכְּלוּ (&apos;ukkÿlu, &quot;they will be fully consumed&quot;); see BDB 571 s.v. מָלֵא. The adverbial sense is rare, appearing elsewhere only in Jer 12:6; thus, the adjectival sense is more probable. The Hebrew word order also suggests the adjectival sense because מָלֵא follows כְּקַשׁ יָבֵשׁ (kÿqash yavesh) rather than אֻכְּלוּ.

50 tn The words &quot;O Nineveh&quot; are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarity. The preceding pronoun is feminine singular, indicating the personified city is in view. See 2:1 (2:2 HT). 51 tn Heb &quot;a counselor of wickedness&quot;; NASB &quot;a wicked counselor&quot;; NAB &quot;the scoundrel planner.&quot;

52 sn Verse 12 begins with a typical prophetic introduction (&quot;This is what the Lord says&quot;) in language similar to the typical ancient Near Eastern messenger formula (see C. Westermann, Basic Forms of Prophetic Speeches, 100-115). This formula is frequently used to introduce prophetic speeches (e.g., Jer 2:5; Ezek 2:4; Amos 1:3). The messenger formula indicates that the prophet&apos;s message is not his own, but is a revelatory and prophetic oracle from the Lord. It confirms the authenticity of the message. 53 tn The syntax of this line is complicated and difficult to translate. The first clause is the concessive protasis of a real condition, while the second is the logical apodosis of a comparative clause. This creates an a fortiori argument: &quot;Even though they are strong and likewise many, so much more will they be cut down and pass away!&quot; The first use of the particle וְכֵן (vÿkhen, &quot;Even though&quot;) introduces a concessive or conditional protasis of a present-time or immediate future-time real condition (R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 87, §515; IBHS 636-37 §38.2). The second use of the particle וְכֵן (&quot;so much more...&quot;) introduces the apodosis of a logical resultative clause (see IBHS 641-42 §38.5). 54 tn Or &quot;are strong&quot; (cf. NCV); or &quot;are at full strength&quot; (NAB, NRSV); or &quot;are intact.&quot; Alternately, &quot;Even though they have allies&quot; (cf. NIV, NLT). The Hebrew noun שְׁלֵמִים (shÿlemim, from שָׁלֵם [shalem]) means &quot;complete, healthy, sound, safe, intact, peaceful&quot; (BDB 1023-24 s.v. שָׁלֵם; HALOT 1538-1539 s.v. שָׁלֵם). It can connote &quot;full strength&quot; or &quot;full number&quot; of an object (Gen 15:16; Deut 25:15; Prov 11:1; Amos 1:6, 9). Most commentators view this as a reference to the strength or numbers of the Assyrian army: &quot;strong&quot; (R. L. Smith, Micah-Malachi [WBC], 77-78), &quot;full strength&quot; (NASB, NRSV) or &quot;intact&quot; (T. Longman, &quot;Nahum,&quot; The Minor Prophets, 2:798). On the other hand, NIV and NLT follow the lead of Wiseman who points out that שְׁלֵמִים can refer to military allies: &quot;Even though they will have allies and so be all the more numerous&quot; (D. J. Wiseman, &quot;Is It Peace? Covenant and Diplomacy,&quot; VT 32 [1982]: 311-26). Nahum refers to the allies of the Assyrians elsewhere (Nah 3:15-17). 55 tn The particle וְכֵן (vÿkhen, &quot;and moreover&quot;) functions as an emphatic comparative adverb of degree (BDB 486 s.v. כֵּן; IBHS 663, 665-67 §39.3.4). It draws a comparison between שְׁלֵמִים (shÿlemim, &quot;strong&quot;) and רַבִּים (rabbim, &quot;many&quot;) but goes one step further for emphasis. This creates an &quot;A, what is more B!&quot; parallelism: &quot;They are strong - what is more - they are many!&quot; 56 tc The MT reads אִם־שְׁלֵמִים וְכֵן רַבִּים (&apos;im-shÿlemim vÿkhen rabbim, &quot;Even though they are strong and numerous&quot;). The complicated syntax of this line led to textual confusion and several textual variants among the versions. For example, the LXX&apos;s κατάρξων ὑδάτων πολλῶν (katarxwn Judatwn pollwn, &quot;ruler of many waters&quot;) reflects מֹשֵׁל מַיִם רַבִּים (moshel mayim rabbim, &quot;ruler of many waters&quot;) which redivides the words, and omits the letter א (aleph) and the word וְכֵן (vÿkhen). Similarly, the Syriac reflects אֶל מֹשְׁלֵי מַיִם רַבִּים (&apos;el mosÿle rabbim, &quot;to the rulers of many waters&quot;). The MT is the most difficult reading and therefore best explains the origin of these textual variants. Moreover, the LXX of Nahum is well-known for its unusual mistranslations of the Hebrew text of Nahum. The LXX butchers v. 12 in several other places (see below). All major English versions follow the MT here. 57 tn The particle וְכֵן (vÿkhen, &quot;so much more...&quot;) introduces the apodosis of a logical resultative clause (IBHS 641-42 §38.5). It emphasizes that the action described in the apodosis will occur almost immediately (e.g., 1 Kgs 20:40; Ps 48:6). 58 tn Heb &quot;they will be sheared.&quot; The term &quot;cut off&quot; (גָּזָז, gazaz) is ordinarily used to describe the literal actions of &quot;shearing&quot; sheep (Gen 31:19; 38:12-13; Deut 15:19; 18:4; 1 Sam 25:2, 4, 7, 11; 2 Sam 13:23-24; Job 31:20; Isa 53:7) and &quot;cutting&quot; hair (Jer 7:29; Mic 1:16; Job 1:20). It is used figuratively here to describe the destruction of the Assyrian army (BDB 159 s.v. גָּזַז; HALOT 186 s.v. גזז). sn The expression they will be cut off is an example of a hypocatastasis (implied comparison); Nahum intentionally chose this term to compare the destruction of the Assyrians to the shearing of sheep. This word-play has great rhetorical impact because the Assyrians frequently used sheep imagery when boasting of the ease and brutality with which they defeated their enemies (see D. Marcus, &quot;Animal Similes in Assyrian Royal Inscriptions,&quot; Or 46 [1977]: 92-93). It is both appropriate (poetic justice) and ironic (reversal of situation) that the Assyrians themselves should suffer a fate which they boasted of inflicting upon others. They will be an easy, helpless prey for the Divine Warrior. Their punishment will fit their crimes. 59 tc In v. 12 the MT preserves a string of plural forms followed by a seemingly anomalous singular form: וְעָבָר...נָגֹזּוּ...רַבִּים...שְׁלֵמִים (shÿlemim ... rabbim ... nagozzu ... vÿ&apos;avar, &quot;Even though they are numerous...they are many...they will be cut off...and he [?] will pass away&quot;). Several other versions (LXX, Syr, Targum) read the plural form וְעָבָרוּ (vÿ&apos;avaru, &quot;and they will pass away&quot;). Several scholars emend the MT to the plural form, noting that the next word (וְעִנִּתִךְ, vÿ&apos;innitikh) begins with vav (ו); they suggest that the plural ending of וְעָבָרוּ dropped out due to haplography or faulty word division (e.g., T. Longman, &quot;Nahum,&quot; The Minor Prophets, 2:798). Another scholar retains the consonantal text, but repoints the form as an infinitive absolute: &quot;They will be cut off, passing away&quot; (K. J. Cathcart). On the other hand, more conservative scholars defend the MT reading and try to solve the problem by suggesting a shift from a plural referent (the Assyrians) to a singular referent (God or the Assyrian king): &quot;They shall be cut down, when he passes through&quot; (KJV) and &quot;They will be cut off and he will pass over&quot; (R. L. Smith, Micah-Malachi [WBC], 77). Still others suggest that the singular form functions as a collective: &quot;They will be cut off and [they] will pass away&quot; (W. A. Maier, Nahum, 206; K&D 27:15). However, rather than resorting to textual emendations or performing syntactical improbabilities, the best solution may be simply to posit the presence of a rhetorical, stylistic device. The shift from these plural forms to the concluding singular form may be an example of heterosis of the plural to the singular (see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 525 [4.5]). This is a common poetic device used for emphasis, especially at the climactic point in a speech (e.g., Gen 29:27; Num 22:6; 32:25; Job 12:7; 18:2; Esth 9:23; Ps 73:7; Prov 14:1, 9; John 3:11; 1 Tim 2:15). tn Or &quot;pass away.&quot; The term עָבַר (&apos;avar, &quot;to pass through&quot;) is a key word in Nahum 1; it occurs three times (Nah 1:8, 12, 15 [2:1 HT]). This verb is often used in reference to water, both the raging onset of flood waters (Nah 1:8) and the passive trickling or dwindling away of receding waters (Job 6:15; 11:16). sn The phrase trickle away is an example of a hypocatastasis (implied comparison); Nahum compares the destruction of the mighty Assyrians with the trickling away of once high waters. This imagery has strong rhetorical impact because the Assyrians often boasted that they overwhelmed their enemies like a flood. It is ironic then that they would soon dwindle away to a mere trickle! This is also an appropriate image in the light of the historical destruction of Nineveh through the use of flood waters, as predicted by the prophet (Nah 2:7-9) and recorded by ancient historians (Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 2.26-27; Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.12; also see P. Haupt, &quot;Xenophon&apos;s Account of the Fall of Nineveh,&quot; JAOS 28 [1907]: 99-107). 60 tn The terms אֲעַנֵּךְ (&apos;a&apos;annekh, &quot;I will [no longer] afflict you&quot;) and וְעִנִּתִךְ (vÿ&apos;innitikh, &quot;I afflicted you&quot;) are both derived from the root II עָנָה (&apos;anah, &quot;to afflict&quot;). The LXX mistakenly confused this with the more common root I עָנָה (&quot;to answer, respond&quot;). Although it mistranslated the roots, the LXX reflects the same consonantal text as the MT: וְעִנִּתִךְ לֹא אֲעַנֵּךְ (vÿ&apos;innitikh lo&apos; &apos;a&apos;annekh, &quot;Although I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no longer&quot;). Some modern English versions supply various terms not in the Hebrew text to indicate the addressee: NIV &quot;O Judah&quot;; NLT &quot;O my people.&quot; Judah is specifically addressed in 1:15 (2:1 HT) and the feminine singular is used there, just as it is in 1:12.

61 tn The particle וְעַתָּה (vÿ&apos;attah, &quot;And now&quot;) often introduces a transition in a prophetic oracle (HALOT 902 s.v. 3.a). It often draws a contrast between a past condition (as described in v. 12) and what will happen in the immediate future (as described in v. 13; see, e.g., Gen 11:6; 2 Sam 2:6; 2 Kgs 12:8). See H. A. Brongers, &quot;Bemerkungen zum Gebrauch des adverbialen we&apos;attah im Alten Testament,&quot; VT 15 (1965): 289-99. 62 tn Heb &quot;his&quot;; the referent (Assyria) has been supplied from context. 63 tc The BHS editors propose revocalizing the MT מֹטֵהוּ (motehu, &quot;his yoke bar&quot;) to מַטַּהַוּ (mattahu, &quot;his scepter&quot;). The threat of breaking an enemy&apos;s scepter was a common ancient Near Eastern treaty curse (see D. Hillers, Treaty-Curses and the Old Testament Prophets [BibOr], 61). This proposed revocalization has no external support. The MT is supported by the use of the parallel word pair מוֹטָה/מוֹסֵר (motah, &quot;scepter&quot;/moser, &quot;bonds&quot;) elsewhere (Jer 27:2). The term מוֹטָה is never used in parallelism with מוֹסֵר elsewhere. sn The terms yoke bar and shackles are figures of speech (hypocatastasis) for Assyrian subjugation of Judah. The imagery of the yoke bar draws an implied comparison between the yoking of a beast of burden to the subjugation of a nation under a foreign power, i.e., vassaldom (Lev 26:13; Jer 27:2; 28:14; Ezek 30:18; 34:27). This imagery also alludes to the Assyrian use of &quot;yoke&quot; imagery to describe their subjugation of foreign nations to the status of vassal. When describing their subjugation of nations, Assyrian rulers frequently spoke of causing them to &quot;pull my yoke.&quot; Sennacherib subjugated Judah to the Assyrian &quot;yoke&quot; in 701 b.c. when he invaded Judah and forced Hezekiah into a position of Assyrian vassal: &quot;I laid waste the large district of Judah and put the straps of my yoke upon Hezekiah, its king&quot; (&quot;Sennacherib: The Siege of Jerusalem,&quot; lines 13-15, in ANET 288). 64 tn Heb &quot;from you&quot;; the word &quot;neck&quot; is supplied in the translation as a clarification for the modern reader who may be less familiar with the imagery of a yoke around the neck of farm animals or draft animals. sn The statement I will break Assyria&apos;s yoke bar from your neck draws an implied comparison (hypocatastasis) between breaking a plowing yoke off the neck of a farming animal and freeing a vassal from the tyranny of an oppressive suzerain through military conquest (Lev 26:13; Isa 58:6; Jer 30:8; Ezek 30:18; 34:27). 65 sn The phrase the shackles that are on you draws an implied comparison between the chains and stocks of prisoners or slaves with the burden of international vassaldom to a tyrannical suzerain who demands absolute obedience and requires annual tributary offerings (e.g., Ps 2:3; Isa 52:2; Jer 27:2; 30:8). &quot;Shackles&quot; were the agent of covenantal discipline (e.g., Deut 28:48). Isaiah stated that the Assyrian &quot;yoke&quot; was the Lord&apos;s instrument of discipline (Isa 28:22). The phrase I will tear apart the shackles that are on you draws an implied comparison (hypocatastasis) between removing the iron chains from a prisoner/slave and freeing a vassal from the oppression of a tyrannical suzerain through military conquest (Ps 2:3; Isa 52:2). 66 tn Heb &quot;your shackles.&quot;

67 tn Heb &quot;has commanded concerning you.&quot; The referent of the 2nd person masculine singular suffix (&quot;you&quot;) probably refers to the Assyrian king (cf. 3:18-19) rather than to the personified city of Nineveh (so NIV). Elsewhere in the book of Nahum, the city of Nineveh is referred to by the feminine rather than masculine gender. Some modern English versions supply terms not in the Hebrew text to indicate the addressee more clearly: NIV &quot;Nineveh&quot;; NLT &quot;the Assyrians in Nineveh.&quot; 68 tn Heb &quot;from your name there will no longer be sown.&quot; 69 tn The MT reading אָשִׂים קִבְרֶךָ (&apos;asim qivrekha, &quot;I will make your grave&quot;) is usually understood as a figure of speech (metonymy of effect) meaning that the Lord will destroy/execute the Assyrian king. On the other hand, the Targum and Syriac treat this as a double-accusative construction - the implied second object of אָשִׂים being מִבֵּית אֱלֹהֶיךָ (mibbet &apos;elohekha, &quot;the house [i.e., &quot;temple&quot;] of your gods&quot;): &quot;I will make it [the house (i.e., temple) of your gods] your grave.&quot; Cathcart suggests revocalizing the MT אָשִׂים to a Hiphil imperfect אָשִׁיִם (&apos;ashiyim) from שָׁמֵם (shamem, &quot;to devastate&quot;): &quot;I will devastate your grave.&quot; Cathcart notes that the destruction of one&apos;s grave, like the threat of no burial, was a common ancient Near Eastern treaty-curse: &quot;Tombs, especially royal tombs, were often protected by curses directed against persons who might violate and desecrate them, and the very curse kings used to have inscribed on their tombs were precisely the curse of no progeny and no resting-place&quot; (K. J. Cathcart, &quot;Treaty-Curses and the Book of Nahum,&quot; CBQ 35 [1973]: 180-81). This might reflect the background of the ancient Near Eastern kudurru curses which were made against those who might devastate a royal grave and which were put into effect by the gods of the king (see F. C. Fensham, &quot;Common Trends in Curses of the Near Eastern Treaties and Kudurru-Inscriptions Compared with Maledictions of Amos and Isaiah,&quot; ZAW 75 [1963]: 157-59). Despite the fact the king&apos;s grave was allegedly protected by the Assyrian gods, the Lord would nevertheless successfully destroy it, and it would be the Assyrian king who would receive the curse. This approach respects the traditional consonantal text and only involves the revocalization of the MT&apos;s שׂ (sin) to שׁ (shin). 70 tn The Hebrew verb קַלֹּוֹתָ (qallota) is usually rendered &quot;you are despised&quot; (e.g., Gen 16:4-5; 1 Sam 2:30). However, it is possible that the Hebrew root קָלַל (qalal) is related to the Assyrian term qalu &quot;accursed&quot; (W. von Soden, &quot;Hebraische Wortforschung,&quot; VTSup 16 [1967]: 295).

71 sn Beginning with 1:15, the verse numbers through 2:13 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 1:15 ET = 2:1 HT, 2:1 ET = 2:2 HT, etc., through 2:13 ET = 2:14 HT. Beginning with 3:1, the verse numbers in the English Bible and the Hebrew Bible are again the same. 72 tn Heb &quot;the feet of a herald.&quot; 73 tn Heb &quot;a messenger of peace.&quot; The Hebrew noun translated &quot;peace&quot; is sometimes used in reference to deliverance or freedom from enemy attack or destruction (e.g., Jer 4:10; 6:14; 8:11; 12:5; 28:9; 29:7). 74 sn The sacred vows to praise God were often made by Israelites as a pledge to proclaim the mercy of the Lord if he would be gracious to deliver (e.g., Gen 28:20; 31:13; Lev 7:16; Judg 11:30, 39; 1 Sam 1:11, 21; 2 Sam 15:7-8; Pss 22:25 [26]; 50:14; 56:12 [13]; 61:5 [6], 8 [9]; 65:1 [2]; 66:13; 116:14, 18; Eccl 5:4 [3]; Jonah 1:16; 2:9 [10]). The words &quot;to praise God&quot; are not in the Hebrew, but are added in the translation for clarification. 75 tc The LXX reflects the plural יוֹסִיפוּ (yosifu, &quot;they shall [never]&quot;). The MT reads the singular יוֹסִיף (yosif, &quot;he shall [never]&quot;) which is also found in the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QpNah). The subject of the verb is the singular noun בְּלִיַּעַל (bÿliyya&apos;al, &quot;the wicked one&quot;) which is also misunderstood by the LXX (see below). 76 tc The MT reads בְּלִיַּעַל (bÿliyya&apos;al, &quot;the wicked one&quot;; so ASV, NASB). The LXX reading εἰς παλαίωσιν (ei&quot; palaiwsin, &quot;to old age&quot;) mistakenly derived בְּלִיַּעַל from בָּלָה (balah, &quot;to become worn&quot;). There are several places in the book of Nahum where the LXX produced poor translations. tn Heb &quot;the wicked one.&quot; This is a collective singular and has been translated as a plural. 77 tn The term &quot;Assyrians&quot; is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied from context for clarity. If left unspecified, the prophetic statement could be understood to mean that the wicked [i.e., wicked conquerors in general] would never again invade Judah. Cf. NLT &quot;your enemies from Nineveh.&quot; 78 tn Or &quot;pass through you&quot; (NASB); or &quot;march against you&quot;; NCV &quot;attack you.&quot; 79 tn Heb &quot;he.&quot; This is in agreement with the singular &quot;wicked one&quot; in the previous line. 80 tn Heb &quot;he is completely cut off.&quot;

1 tn The introductory phrase &quot;The watchmen of Nineveh shout&quot; is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied from the context for clarity. 2 tc The MT reads מֵפִיץ (mefits, &quot;scatterer, disperser&quot;), the Hiphil participle of פּוּץ (puts, &quot;to scatter, to disperse&quot;; HALOT 755 s.v. פוּץ, but see BDB 807 s.v. מֵפִיץ, which classifies it as a noun). The Vulgate&apos;s qui dispergat (&quot;one who disperses&quot;) and the LXX&apos;s ἐμφυσῶν (emfuswn, &quot;one who blows hard; one who scatters&quot;) also reflect מֵפִיץ. The BHS editors propose the emendation מַפֵּץ (mappets, &quot;shatterer, hammerer, war club&quot;; e.g., Jer 51:20 and Prov 25:18). This is unnecessary; the text makes sense as it stands and there is no textual support for the emendation. The theme of exile and dispersion is prominent in the book (Nah 2:7; 3:10-11, 17-18). tn Heb &quot;a scatterer.&quot; The Hebrew term מֵפִיץ (mefits, &quot;scatterer&quot;) is either a collective singular referring to the Babylonian army or a singular of number referring to the Babylonian commander. Singular forms occur elsewhere in the vision of the fall of Nineveh (2:1-10), used in reference to the Babylonian commander (Nah 2:3, 5) 3 tn Or &quot;has come up&quot;; or &quot;has advanced.&quot; Used in reference to an army, the verb עָלָה (&apos;alah, &quot;to go up&quot;) means &quot;to advance; to march against&quot; (HALOT 829 s.v. 3.d; see 1 Sam 7:7; 1 Kgs 20:22; Isa 7:1; 21:2; Jer 46:9; Joel 1:6; Mic 2:3). Appearing in a prophetic vision, the suffix conjugation (perfect tense) form עָלָה can denote a future-time action that is pictured as complete (certain) and independent (not contingent upon other factors). The so-called &quot;prophetic perfect&quot; or &quot;perfect of confidence&quot; vividly expresses a future action that is &quot;as good as done&quot; (cf. Num 24:17; Isa 5:13; 8:23-9:1). See R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 33, §165; IBHS 489-90 §30.5.1. 4 tn Heb &quot;against your face&quot;; NASB, NRSV &quot;against you.&quot; 5 tn The Qal infinitive absolute נָצוֹר (notsar, from נָצַר [nastar], &quot;to guard&quot;) is used in an imperatival sense as the following string of imperatives suggests. The imperatival use of the infinitive absolute is often used to introduce a series of imperatives with special urgency (e.g., Deut 1:16; 2 Sam 24:12; 2 Kgs 5:10). See IBHS 593-94 §35.5.1; R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 42, §211. 6 tc The BHS editors suggest revocalizing the Masoretic noun מְצֻרָה (mÿtsurah, &quot;rampart&quot;) to the noun מַצָּרָה (matsarah, &quot;the watchtower&quot;) from the root נָצַר (natsar, &quot;to watch, guard&quot;). This would create a repetition of the root נָצַר which immediately precedes it: מַצָּרָה נָצוֹר (natsor matsarah, &quot;Watch the watchtower!&quot;). However, the proposed noun מַצָּרָה (&quot;the watchtower&quot;) appears nowhere in the Hebrew Bible. On the other hand, the Masoretic reading מְצֻרָה (&quot;rampart&quot;) and the related noun מָצוֹר (matsor, &quot;rampart&quot;) appear often (Pss 31:22; 60:11; Hab 2:1; Zech 9:3; 2 Chr 8:5; 11:5, 10, 11, 23; 12:4; 14:5, 21:3; 32:10). Thus, the Masoretic vocalization should be preserved. The LXX completely misunderstood this line. The LXX reading (&quot;one who delivers out of tribulation&quot;) has probably arisen from a confusion of the MT noun נָצוֹר (&quot;guard&quot;) with the common verb נָצַר (&quot;deliver&quot;). It also reflects a confusion of MT מְצֻרָה (&quot;road, rampart&quot;) with מִצְּרָה (mitsÿrah, &quot;from distress&quot;). 7 tn Heb &quot;Make strong your loins,&quot; an expression which could refer (1) to the practice of tucking the ends of the long cloak (outer garment) into the belt to shorten it in preparation for activities like running, fighting in battle, etc. (cf. NAB, NRSV &quot;gird your loins&quot;); (2) to preparing oneself physically for the onslaught of the enemy (cf. NASB &quot;strengthen your back&quot;); or (3) to a combination of mental and physical preparation for battle (cf. NIV &quot;brace yourselves&quot;). 8 tn Heb &quot;Make [your] strength exceedingly firm.&quot;

9 tn The Qal perfect שָׁב (shav, &quot;restore, return&quot;) is an example of the so-called &quot;prophetic perfect.&quot; In this case, the perfect tense does not denote past-time action, but a future-time action that is pictured as complete (certain) and independent (not contingent upon other factors). The so-called &quot;prophetic perfect&quot; or &quot;perfect of confidence&quot; vividly expresses a future action that is deemed &quot;as good as done&quot; (Num 24:17; Isa 5:13; 8:23-9:1). See R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 33, §165; IBHS 489-90 §30.5.1. Though the transitive use of the Qal of this verb is problematic, most scholars derive שָׁב from the root שׁוּב (shuv, &quot;to turn, to return, to restore&quot;). However, W. A. Maier (Nahum, 232) contends that שָׁב is derived from I שָׁבַב (shavav, &quot;to cut off, to destroy, to smite&quot;) which is related to Arabic sabba (&quot;to cut&quot;), Aramaic sibba&apos;(&quot;splinter&quot;), and New Hebrew. Maier admits that this would be the only occurrence of a verb from I שָׁבָב in the OT; however, he argues that the appearance of the plural noun שְׁבָבִים (shÿvavim, &quot;splinters&quot;) in Hos 8:6 provides adequate support. There are several problems with Maier&apos;s proposal. First, his support from Arabic, Aramaic (Targum) and New Hebrew is all late. Second, it creates a hapax legomenon (a word that occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible) for a well-known Hebrew word which frequently appears in climactic contexts in prophetic speeches, as here. Third, the root שׁוּב (shuv, &quot;to turn, to return, to restore&quot;) makes perfectly good sense in this context. The meaning of this usage of שָׁב (from the root שׁוּב) is debated. The LXX took it in the negative sense &quot;has turned aside.&quot; On the other hand, it is nuanced in a positive, salvific sense by the Vulgate, Targum, and Syriac. The salvific nuance is best for the following reasons: (1) its direct object is גְּאוֹן (ge&apos;on) which should be understood in the positive sense of &quot;majesty; exaltation; glory&quot; (see following note on the word &quot;majesty&quot;); (2) the motive clause introduced by causative/ explanatory כִּי (ki, &quot;for&quot;) would make little sense, saying that the reason the Lord was about to destroy Nineveh was because he had turned away the pride of Judah; however, it makes good sense to say that the Lord would destroy Nineveh because he was about to deliver Judah; and (3) a reference to the Lord turning aside from Judah would be out of harmony with the rest of the book. 10 tc The BHS editors propose emending the MT reading גְּאוֹן (gÿ&apos;on, &quot;majesty; pride&quot;) to גֶּפֶן (gefen, &quot;vineyard&quot;) due to the mention of &quot;their branches&quot; (וּזְמֹרֵיהֶם, uzÿmorehem) in the following line (so HALOT 169 s.v. גָּאוֹן [2.b]). However, the LXX supports the MT. tn While גְּאוֹן (ge&apos;on) sometimes has the negative connotation &quot;pride; arrogance; presumption&quot; (Isa 13:11, 19; 14:11; 16:6; 23:9; Jer 13:9; 48:29; Ezek 16:49, 56; 32:12; Hos 5:5; 7:10; Amos 6:8; Zeph 2:10; Zech 9:6; 10:11; 11:3; Ps 59:13; Job 35:12; 40:10), it probably has the positive connotation &quot;eminence; majesty; glory&quot; (e.g., as in Exod 15:7; Isa 2:10, 19, 21; 4:2; 24:14; 60:15; Mic 5:3; Ps 47:5) in this context (BDB 145 s.v. 1.a). 11 tn The preposition כְּ (kaf) on כִּגְאוֹן (kig&apos;on, &quot;the glory of Israel&quot;) may be comparative (&quot;like the glory of Israel&quot;) or emphatic (&quot;the glory of Jacob, indeed, the glory of Israel&quot;). See J. O&apos;Rourke, &quot;Book Reviews and Short Notes: Review of Nahum in the Light of Northwest Semitic by Kevin J. Cathcart,&quot; CBQ 36 (1974): 397. 12 tn Or &quot;for.&quot; The introductory particle כִּי (ki) may be causal (&quot;because&quot;), explanatory (&quot;for&quot;), or concessive (&quot;although&quot;). KJV adopts the causal sense (&quot;For&quot;), while the concessive sense (&quot;Although&quot;) is adopted by NASB, NIV, NJPS, NRSV. 13 tn Heb &quot;plunderers have plundered them.&quot; The Hebrew root בָּקַק (baqaq, &quot;to lay waste, to empty&quot;) is repeated for emphasis: בְקָקוּם בֹּקְקִים (vÿqaqum boqÿqim, &quot;plunderers have plundered them&quot;). Similar repetition of the root בָּקַק occurs in Isa 24:3: &quot;[The earth] will be completely laid waste&quot; (הִבּוֹק תִּבּוֹק, hibboq tibboq). 14 tn Heb &quot;their vine-branches.&quot; The term &quot;vine-branches&quot; is a figurative expression (synecdoche of part for the whole) representing the agricultural fields as a whole.

15 tc The MT reads מְאָדָּם (mÿ&apos;adam, &quot;reddened&quot;) from אָדֹם (&apos;adom, &quot;red&quot;). The LXX confused the roots אָדָם (&quot;man&quot;) and אָדֹם (&quot;red&quot;): ἐξ ἀνθρώπων (ex anqrwpwn, &quot;from among men&quot;) which reflects מֵאָדָם (me&apos;adam, &quot;from man&quot;) from אָדָם. tn The Hebrew term מְאָדָּם (&quot;reddened&quot;) from אָדֹם (&quot;red&quot;) refers to clothes made red with dye (Exod 25:6; 26:14; 35:7, 23; 36:13; 39:34) or made red from bloodshed (Isa 63:2). The parallelism between מְאָדָּם (&quot;reddened&quot;) and מְתֻלָּעִים (mÿtulla&apos;im, &quot;clad in scarlet colored clothing&quot;) suggests that the shields were dyed prior to battle, like the scarlet dyed uniforms. Nahum 2:1-10 unfolds the assault in chronological sequence; thus, the spattering of blood on the warrior&apos;s shields would be too early in the account (R. D. Patterson, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah [WEC], 65). sn As psychological warfare, warriors often wore uniforms colored blood-red, to strike fear into the hearts of their enemy (see Xenophon, Cyropaedia 6.4.1; Ezek 23:5-6). 16 tn The Pual participle מְתֻלָּעִים (mÿtulla&apos;im, &quot;dressed in scarlet&quot;) from תָּלָע (tala&apos;, &quot;scarlet&quot;) is used elsewhere of clothing dyed red or purple (Isa 1:18; Lam 4:5). 17 tc The MT reads פְּלָדוֹת (pÿladot, &quot;steel&quot;; see the following tn). The LXX&apos;s αἱ ἡνιάι (Jai Jhniai, &quot;the reins&quot;) and Vulgate&apos;s habenai (&quot;reins&quot;) confused פְּלָדוֹת (pÿladot) with כְּלָיוֹת (kÿlayot, &quot;reins, kidneys&quot;). The BHS editors suggest emending the MT&apos;s פְּלָדוֹת (peladot) to לַפִּדוֹת (lappidot, &quot;torches&quot;) to create the simile כְּאֵשׁ לַפִּדוֹת (kÿ&apos;esh lappidot, &quot;like torches of fire&quot; or &quot;like flaming torches&quot;) which is reflected in the Syriac Peshitta and Symmachus (so KJV, RSV, NJPS). The problem with this is that לַפִּיד (lappid, &quot;torch&quot;) is masculine in gender, so the plural form is not לַפִּדוֹת but לַפִּדִים (lappidim) - which appears in Nah 2:4 (BDB 542 s.v. לַפִּיד; HALOT 533 s.v. לַפִּיד). Others propose a complete reversal of the consonants to דלפות from the root דָּלַף (dalaf, &quot;to drip, to trickle, to leak, to weep&quot;) and translate כְּאֵשׁ דְלָפוֹת (kÿ&apos;esh dÿlafot) as &quot;like flickering fire&quot; (so NEB). Against this proposal is the fact that דָּלָף is usually used in reference to water, but it is never used in reference to fire (HALOT 223 s.v. דלף; BDB 196 s.v. דָּלַף). tn Heb &quot;the steel.&quot; The Hebrew term פְּלָדוֹת is a hapax legomenon. The corresponding noun פְּלָדָה (pÿladah) probably means &quot;metal, steel&quot; (BDB 811 s.v. פְּלָדָה; HALOT 761 s.v. פְּלָדָה), and it is probably related to Arabic puladu, Syriac pld&apos;, and early Persian fulad (all of which mean &quot;steel&quot;). This rendering is followed by NASB, NIV, NRSV. The term פְּלָדוֹת (&quot;steel&quot;) probably refers to the metallic pole attachments for the chariot spears, the side armor of the chariots, or the steel scythes fastened to the axle of a chariot. Xenophon described the army of Cyrus in a similar manner; the side armor of the chariots and the breastplates and thigh-pieces of the chariot-horses were &quot;flashing with bronze&quot; (Xenophon, Cyropaedia 6.4.1). On the other hand, Cathcart connects Hebrew פְּלָדָה to Ugaritic paladu, which means &quot;a garment made of linen hair,&quot; and suggests that פְּלָדוֹת הָרֶכֶב (pÿladot harekhev) refers to the coverings, blankets, or caparisons of chariot horses (K. J. Cathcart, Nahum in the Light of Northwest Semitic [BibOr], 88). This demands that הָרֶכֶב be nuanced &quot;chariot horses&quot; - a problem when it means &quot;chariots&quot; in Nah 2:4; 3:2. 18 tn The collective singular רֶכֶב (rekhev, &quot;chariot&quot;) refers to all of the chariots in the army as a whole: &quot;chariots; chariotry&quot; (BDB 939 s.v. 1; HALOT 891 s.v. 1). The singular form rarely refers to a single chariot (BDB 939 s.v. 2; HALOT 891 s.v. 3). The collective use is indicated by the plural verb &quot;they race back and forth&quot; (יִתְהוֹלְלוּ, yitholÿlu) in v. 5 (GKC 462 §145.b). The term רֶכֶב usually refers to war chariots (Exod 14:7; Josh 11:4; 17:16, 18; 24:6; Judg 1:19; 4:3, 7, 13; 5:28; 1 Sam 13:5; 2 Sam 1:6; 8:4; 10:18; 1 Kgs 9:19, 22; 10:26; Jer 47:3; 50:37; 51:21; Ezek 23:24; Nah 2:3, 4, 13). 19 tc The MT reads the preposition בְּ (bet, &quot;are [like]&quot;), but several Hebrew mss read the comparative preposition כְּ (kaf, &quot;like&quot;). This textual variant probably arose due to the visual similarity of the two letters (orthographic confusion) and the relatively rare use of בְּ in metaphors - the comparative preposition כְּ (&quot;like&quot;) is much more common in metaphors. The MT is the more difficult reading and best explains the origin of the variant. tn Heb &quot;The chariots are...&quot; The preposition בְּ on בְּאֵשׁ (bÿ&apos;esh) denotes essence: &quot;The chariots are...&quot; (GKC 430 §133.c; HALOT 104 s.v. בְּ 3). The use of this preposition creates a metaphor, comparing the steel fittings of the chariots to flashes of fire. 20 tn Or perhaps &quot;The chariots are [like] flaming torches.&quot; 21 tn Heb &quot;on the day of its preparation.&quot; The Hiphil infinitive construct הֲכִינוֹ (hakhino; from כּוּן, kun) means &quot;to prepare, to make ready&quot; (HALOT 465 s.v. כּוּן; BDB 466 s.v. כּוּן). The Hiphil verb is used of preparing weapons and military equipment for the day of battle (2 Chr 26:14; Ps 7:13 [HT 7:14]; 57:6 [HT 57:7]). The 3rd person masculine singular suffix (&quot;its preparation&quot;) is a collective singular, referring to the chariotry as a whole. 22 tc Some scholars adopt the variant reading הַפְּרֹשִׁים (happÿroshim, &quot;the horses&quot;) and relate הָרְעָלוּ (hor&apos;alu) to Arabic raàala (&quot;to stand in row and rank&quot;): &quot;the horses stand in row and rank,&quot; that is, at attention. However, it is preferable to retain the MT for the noun, with the verb given its normal Hebrew meaning. tn Heb &quot;the spears quiver&quot;; or &quot;the spears are made to quiver.&quot; Alternately, &quot;the horses quiver&quot; or &quot;the horses shake [with excitement].&quot; The Hophal perfect הָרְעָלוּ (hor&apos;alu, &quot;are made to quiver&quot;) is from רָעַל (ra&apos;al, &quot;to quiver, to shake&quot;) which appears elsewhere only in Hab 2:16 (BDB 947 s.v. רָעַל; HALOT 900 s.v. II רעל); the related noun רַעַל (&quot;reeling&quot;) appears only once (Zech 12:2). This Hebrew root is related to the Aramaic רְעַל (rÿ&apos;al, &quot;to quiver, to shake&quot;). The action of the spear-shafts quivering is metonymical (effect for cause) to the action of the spear-shafts being brandished by the warriors. In the translation the words &quot;the soldiers&quot; are supplied for clarity. 23 tc The MT reads הַבְּרֹשִׁים (habbÿroshim, &quot;the cypresses&quot;). A variant textual tradition (preserved in several Hebrew mss) reads הַפְּרֹשִׁים (happÿroshim, &quot;spears, horses, horsemen&quot;) which is reflected in the LXX and Syriac. The variant noun הַפְּרֹשִׁים is derived either from IV פָּרַשׁ (&quot;horse, horseman&quot;; see BDB 831 s.v. פָּרַשׁ; HALOT 977 s.v. פָּרָשׁ) or II פָּרַשׁ (&quot;spear, staff&quot;) which is related to Akkadian parussu (&quot;spear-staff&quot;; see BDB 831 II פָּרַשׁ). The LXX connects הַבְּרֹשִׁים to IV פָּרַשׁ (&quot;horsemen&quot;) as indicated by its translation οἱ ἱππεϊς (Joi Jippei&quot;, &quot;the horsemen&quot;). While some English versions follow the MT (KJV, NASB, NIV, NJPS), others adopt the alternate textual tradition (RSV, NEB, NJB, NRSV). tn Heb &quot;the cypresses&quot;; alternately, &quot;the horses.&quot; The Hebrew noun הַבְּרֹשִׁים (&quot;the cypresses&quot;) is probably from the root בְּרוֹשׁ (bÿrosh, &quot;cypress, fir&quot;) and is a figure of speech (synecdoche of material) in which the thing made (spear-shafts) is intended by the use of the term for the material out of which it is made (cypress wood). See K. J. Cathcart, Nahum in the Light of Northwest Semitic (BibOr), 89.

1 tn Heb &quot;of bloods.&quot; The plural noun דָּמִים (damim, &quot;bloods&quot;) connotes &quot;bloodshed&quot; or &quot;blood guilt&quot; (BDB 196-97 s.v. דָּם 2.f; HALOT 224-25 s.v. דָּם 5; DCH 2:443-47 s.v. דָּם). Human blood in its natural state in the body is generally designated by the singular form דָּם (dam, &quot;blood&quot;); after it has been spilled, the plural form is used to denote the abundance of blood in quantity (IBHS 119-20 §7.4.1; BDB 196-97 s.v. דָּם 2.f). The plural is often used with the verb שָׁפַךְ (shafakh, &quot;to spill, to shed&quot;) to connote bloodshed (Gen 9:6; 37:22; Lev 17:4; Num 35:33; Deut 21:7; 1 Sam 25:31; 1 Kgs 18:28; 2 Kgs 21:16; 24:4; 1 Chr 22:8; Ezek 16:38; 22:4, 6, 9, 12, 27; 23:45; 33:25; 36:18; Prov 1:16). The plural often denotes bloodshed (Gen 4:10; 2 Sam 3:27, 28; 16:8; 20:12; 1 Kgs 2:5; 2 Kgs 9:7, 26, 33; 2 Chr 24:25; Job 16:18; Isa 1:15; 4:4; 9:4; 26:21; 33:15; 34:3, 6, 7; Ezek 7:23; 16:6, 9, 36; 21:37; 22:13; 24:8; Hos 1:4; 4:2; Hab 2:8, 12, 17; Mic 3:10; Zech 9:7) or blood-guilt (Exod 22:1; Lev 20:9; Num 35:27; Deut 19:10; 22:8; Judg 9:24; 1 Sam 25:26, 33; 2 Sam 21:1; Isa 33:15; Ezek 9:9). The term can refer to murder (2 Sam 16:7, 8; Pss 5:7; 26:9; 55:24; 59:3; 139:10; Prov 29:10) or more generally, connote social injustice, cruelty, and oppression (Deut 21:8, 9; 1 Sam 19:5; 2 Kgs 21:6; 24:4; Pss 94:21; 106:38; Prov 6:17; Isa 59:7; Jer 7:6; 22:3; Joel 4:19; Jonah 1:14). The term may refer to blood that has been shed in war (1 Kgs 2:5) and the unnecessary shedding of blood of one&apos;s enemy (1 Kgs 2:31), which is probably the intended meaning here. The phrase &quot;city of bloodshed&quot; (עִיר דָּמִים [&apos;ir damim], &quot;city of bloods&quot;) is used elsewhere to describe a city held guilty before God of blood-guilt and about to be judged by God (Ezek 22:2; 24:6). 2 tn Heb &quot;All of her [is] lying.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;full of plunder.&quot; 4 tn Heb &quot;prey does not depart.&quot;

5 tn Heb &quot;the sound of a whip.&quot; 6 tn Heb &quot;the shaking of a chariot wheel.&quot; 7 tn Heb &quot;a horse.&quot; 8 tn Albright argues that the term דֹּהֵר (doher) should be translated as &quot;chariot driver&quot; (W. F. Albright, &quot;The Song of Deborah in Light of Archaeology,&quot; BASOR 62 [1936]: 30). More recent research indicates that this term denotes &quot;to dash&quot; (HALOT 215 s.v.) or &quot;to gallop, neigh&quot; (DCH 2:417 s.v. דהר I). It is used as a synonym for רָקַד (raqad, &quot;to skip&quot;). This Hebrew verb is related to Egyptian thr (&quot;to travel by chariot&quot;) and Arabic dahara VII (&quot;to hurry&quot;). The related noun דַּהֲרָה (daharah) means &quot;dashing, galloping&quot; (Judg 5:22; HALOT 215 s.v.; DCH 2:417 s.v. דַּהֲרָה I). 9 tn Heb &quot;a chariot.&quot; 10 tn The Piel participle מְרַקֵּדָה (mÿraqqedah, &quot;jolting&quot;) is from רַקַד (raqad); this verb means &quot;to dance, to leap&quot; (of children, Job 21:11), &quot;to skip about, to dance&quot; (Eccl 3:4), and &quot;to leap&quot; (of chariots, Joel 2:5). In related Semitic languages (Akkadian, Ugaritic, and Arabic) the root raqad means &quot;to dance, to skip about.&quot; Here, the verb is used as a figurative expression (hypocatastasis) to describe the jostling of the madly rushing war-chariots.

11 tn Heb &quot;a horseman.&quot; Although the Hebrew term פָּרָס (paras, alternately spelled פָּרָשׂ [paras] here) could denote &quot;horse&quot; (1 Sam 8:11; Joel 2:4; Hab 1:8; Jer 46:4), the Hiphil participle מַעֲלֶה (ma&apos;aleh, &quot;cause to charge&quot;) - the subject of which is פָּרָס - suggests that פָּרָס refers here to &quot;horsemen&quot; charging their horses (2 Sam 1:6; 1 Kgs 20:20; Jer 4:29; 46:4). 12 tn The term מַעֲלֶה (ma&apos;aleh; the Hiphil participle &quot;cause to charge&quot;) refers to charioteers bringing war-horses up to a charge or attack (e.g., Jer 46:9; 51:27). On the other hand, the KJV translates this as &quot;lifteth up [both the bright sword and the glittering sword],&quot; while RV renders it as &quot;mounts [his horse (or chariot)].&quot; 13 tn Heb &quot;a sword.&quot; 14 tn Heb &quot;flash of a sword.&quot; Alternately, &quot;swords flash.&quot; Although לַהַב (lahav) can mean &quot;blade&quot; (Judg 3:22; 1 Sam 17:7), it means &quot;flash [of the sword]&quot; here (e.g., Hab 3:11; see HALOT 520 s.v.) as suggested by its parallelism with וּבְרַק (uvÿraq, &quot;flashing, gleaming point [of the spear]&quot;); cf. Job 20:25; Deut 32:41; Hab 3:11; Ezek 21:15. 15 tn Heb &quot;a spear.&quot; 16 tn Heb &quot;and flash of a spear.&quot; Alternately, &quot;spears glimmer&quot; (HALOT 162 s.v. בָּרָק). 17 tn Heb &quot;many slain.&quot; 18 tc The MT reads לַגְּוִיָּה (laggÿviyyah, &quot;to the dead bodies&quot;). The LXX reflects לְגוֹיָה (lÿgoyah, &quot;to her nations&quot;) which arose due to confusion between the consonant ו (vav) and the vowel וֹ (holem-vav) in an unpointed text. tn Heb &quot;There is no end to the dead bodies.&quot; 19 tn Heb &quot;they.&quot;

185.content: * Nineveh *  Nineveh stands in Scripture as the representative of apostate religious Gentiledom, as Babylon represents the confusion into which the Gentile political world-system has fallen Daniel 2:41-43, * (See Scofield &quot;Isaiah 13:1&quot;) * , Under the preaching of Jonah, B.C. 862, the city and king had turned to God (Elohim), Jonah 3:3-10 But in the time of Nahum, more than a century later, the city had wholly apostatized from God. It is this which distinguishes Nineveh from all the other ancient Gentile cities, and which makes her the suited symbol of the present religious Gentile world-system in the last day. Morally, Nineveh is described in Romans 1:21-23. The chief deity of apostate Nineveh was the bull-god, with the face of a man and the wings of a bird: &quot;an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and four-footed beasts.&quot;  The message of Nahum, uttered about one hundred years before the destruction of Nineveh, is, therefore, not a call to repentance, but an unrelieved warning of judgment: &quot;He will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time.&quot; Nahum 1:9; see, also, Nahum 3:10. For there is no remedy for apostasy but utter judgment, and a new beginning. Cf. ; Isaiah 1:4,5,24-28; Hebrews 6:4-8; Proverbs 29:1.  It is the way of God; apostasy is punished by catastrophic destruction. Of this the flood and the destruction of Nineveh are witnesses. The coming destruction of apostate Christendom is foreshadowed by these. (Cf) Daniel 2:34,35; Luke 17:26,27; Revelation 19:17-21. * burden * See note 1, * (See Scofield &quot;Isaiah 13:1&quot;) *

* God is jealous *  The great ethical lesson of Nahum is that the character of God makes Him not only &quot;slow to anger,&quot; and &quot;a stronghold to them that trust Him,&quot; but also one who &quot;will not at all acquit the wicked.&quot; He can be &quot;just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus&quot; Romans 3:26 but only because His holy law has been vindicated in the cross.
* he knoweth them that trust * Psalms 1:6; 2 Timothy 2:19 * (See Scofield &quot;Psalms 2:12&quot;) *.  * Nineveh *  * (See Scofield &quot;Nahum 1:1&quot;) *

199.content: The burden - When the prophets were sent to denounce judgments against a nation or city, the word was usually called the burden of that nation or city. The vision - As prophets were of old called seers, 1Sam 9:9, so their prophesies were called visions. Nahum - His name speaks a comforter, but it is God&apos;s people to whom he gives notice of the destruction of their oppressors.
Jealous - For his own glory. Revengeth - As supreme governor, who by office is bound to right the oppressed, and to punish the oppressor.

Hath his way - The methods of his providence. The whirlwind - Which beareth before it all things that stand in its way. The dust of his feet - Though he be surrounded with darkness, yet as an army afar off is discovered by the dust that their feet raise, so wilt God appear with great power marching against his enemies.
The flower - Whatever flourished thereon; the blossoms, and flowers which were wont to be the glory of it.
Knoweth - He approves, owns, and preserves them.

An over - running flood - His judgments like a mighty flood that overflows all banks, shall swallow up Assyria. Thereof - Of Nineveh, that is Nineveh itself. Darkness - Troubles, and desolating afflictions.
Against the Lord - What you imagine or design against his people, ye design against him? Make an utter end - He will bring you to utter desolation.

As thorns - They shall be like thorns easily burnt, and like thorns folded together which burn together, and help to destroy each other. As drunkards - As men drunken, and unable to help themselves, so the Assyrians drunk with pleasure and pride, shall be surprised, and easily overthrown.
Come - Sennacherib, or Rabshekah. Thee - From Nineveh. Against the Lord - Against the people of the Lord, 2Chron 32:1.
They - The Assyrians. Quiet - Be secure, and fear no dangers. Yet thus - Irresistible, suddenly, and universally. He - The angel of the Lord. Thee - O Israel, I will no more use that rod.
Thee - Thee, Sennacherib, and the whole kingdom of Assyria. Be sown - None shall bear thy name, and title; but thy kingdom shall be swallowed up.
Keep - Be careful to serve God. Thy vows - Made in thy distress. The wicked - That wicked oppressor, Sennacherib.
He - The Medes or Chaldeans, that dash Nineveh in pieces. The munition - The forts. Make thy loins strong - Strengthen thyself.

He - The Medes or Chaldeans, that dash Nineveh in pieces. The munition - The forts. Make thy loins strong - Strengthen thyself.
The horsemen - The Chaldeans and their confederates.

The whoredom - The idolatries, which were multiplied by the many people that served the Assyrian idols. And whoredoms literally understood, did undoubtedly abound, where wealth, luxury, ease, and long continuance of these were to be found. Well - favoured - Glorious in their state and government, and in the splendor of their idols, temples, and sacrifices. Of witchcrafts - Bewitching policies; or it may be taken for witchcrafts or necromances, which abounded among the Assyrians. That selleth - That dispose of them as imperiously, and absolutely as men do slaves. And families - This may intimate the seducing of some particular and eminent families to an hereditary service of the Assyrian idols, or to witchcrafts, in which the devil imitated God&apos;s institution, in taking a family to his service.
Discover - l will strip thee naked, and deal with thee as inhuman soldiers deal with captive women.
Shall flee - With loathing and abhorrence. Will bemoan - Whose bowels will be moved for her that had no bowels for any one.

Thou - O Nineveh. No - It is supposed this was what we now called Alexandria. Art thou greater, stronger, and wiser? Yet all her power was broken, her riches spoiled, and her glory buried in ruins. Rampart - The defence of its walls on one side. Her wall - A mighty, strong wall, built from the sea landward.

Her strength - Furnishing soldiers and warlike assistance. It was infinite - There was no end to their confidence and warlike provisions. Put - Or the Moors, who lie westward of Alexandria. Lubim - The people that inhabited that which is now called Cyrene.
Thou also - Thou shalt drink deep of the bitter cup of God&apos;s displeasure. Hid - Thou shalt hide thyself. O Nineveh, as well as Alexandria. Shalt seek - Shalt sue for, and intreat assistance.
Ripe figs - Whose weight and ripeness will bring them quickly to the ground. Shaken - If but lightly touched.
Are women - Were very cowards. The gates - The strong frontiers. Wide open - Either through fear or treachery. Thy bars - With which the gates were shut and strengthened.
Draw thee waters - Fill all thy cisterns, and draw the waters into the ditches. Tread the mortar - Set thy brick - makers on work to prepare store of materials for thy fortifications.
There - In the very fortresses. Eat thee - As easily as the canker - worm eats the green herb. Many - They are innumerable; be thou so if thou canst; all will be to no purpose.
The canker - worm spoileth - So these are like the canker - worms, which spoil wherever they come, and when no more is to be gotten, flee away.

Thy crowned - Thy confederate kings and princes. Captains - Commanders and officers are for number, like locusts and grasshoppers; but &apos;tis all for shew, not for help. In the cool day - While the season suits them. The sun - When trouble, war, and danger, like the parching sun, scald them. Is not known - Thou shalt never know where to find them.
Thy shepherds - Thy rulers and counsellors. Slumber - Are remiss, heartless, or dead. No man gathereth - No one will concern himself to preserve thy dispersed ones.
Shall clap the hands - Insulting and rejoicing. Thy wickedness - Thy tyranny, pride, oppression and cruelty; treading down and trampling upon them.
